## Add baseline predictors

Use `outcome ~ time + covariates`, with time first. The package fits
respondent-level OLS separately in every rolling and final pre-event window.
Numeric covariates enter linearly. Factors, character, and logical columns are
categorical indicators; ordered factors are treated as unordered. Formula
transformations, interactions, and nonlinear time trends remain unsupported.

This simulation deliberately adds a strong baseline predictor and changing
survey composition, so the role of adjustment can be checked against a known
effect. These are synthetic observations, not an empirical application.

```{r setup}
library(eventsurvey)
set.seed(926)
survey <- data.frame(day = rep(-24:6, each = 100))
survey$baseline <- rnorm(nrow(survey), mean = 0.7 * sin(survey$day / 3))
survey$group <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), length.out = nrow(survey)))
survey$y <- 10 + 0.1 * survey$day + 3 * survey$baseline +
  0.8 * (survey$group == "B") + 2 * (survey$day >= 0) +
  rnorm(nrow(survey))

time_only <- eventsurvey(y ~ day, survey)
adjusted <- eventsurvey(y ~ day + baseline + group, survey)
adjusted
```

The true event effect is two outcome units in every post-event period. The
baseline variables describe characteristics that the event cannot change.
In real data, measurement after the event is acceptable only if the variable
still records an unaffected baseline characteristic; a contemporaneous
attitude or behavior changed by the event is not an appropriate control.

## Compare predictive performance

Compare models on the same observations and with the same windows. If any
candidate covariate is missing, construct a common complete-case sample before
fitting both models. Automatic omission otherwise changes the comparison.

```{r comparison}
comparison <- data.frame(
  model = c("Time only", "Baseline-adjusted"),
  effect = c(coef(time_only), coef(adjusted)),
  standard_error = c(time_only$estimate$std_error, adjusted$estimate$std_error),
  reference_rmse = c(
    sqrt(mean(time_only$reference$error^2)),
    sqrt(mean(adjusted$reference$error^2))
  ),
  bias_bound = c(time_only$estimate$bias_bound, adjusted$estimate$bias_bound)
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The rolling RMSE describes the same pre-event forecasting exercises for both
models. Their errors overlap and are not independent validation observations.
Lower in-sample RMSE alone is insufficient: adding weak predictors can make
forecasts less stable, and adjusted intervals need not be narrower. Choose
covariates from substantive knowledge before examining post-event results.
Repeatedly tuning a specification on the rolling errors introduces selection
uncertainty that the reported intervals do not include.

```{r diagnostics}
adjusted$model_diagnostics
plot(adjusted, type = "diagnostics")
```

## What is predicted and averaged?

For each forecast date, the fitted pre-event model predicts the outcome for
each respondent actually observed on that date, using that respondent's
covariates. The counterfactual mean averages those predictions. The period
effect subtracts that mean from the observed outcome mean; the window effect
averages the period effects with equal weight.

```{r counterfactual}
plot(adjusted, type = "counterfactual")
```

The adjusted path can bend because covariate composition changes, even though
time enters the regression linearly. A causal interpretation requires a
credible no-event conditional outcome model and a defensible relation between
interview timing, baseline covariates, and potential outcomes. The target is
the average effect for each forecast date's respondent population. A common
population ATE needs additional representativeness or standardization
assumptions. Covariates do not remove an unrelated contemporaneous shock or
automatically repair event-induced nonresponse.

## Uncertainty and practical requirements

The adjusted covariance calculation combines respondent influence functions
for every effect and rolling reference error. It includes fitted coefficients,
each forecast period's estimated covariate mean, and all shared-observation
covariances needed for the intervals. Scores are centered within interview
period, with covariance correction `n / (n - 1)`, conditional on period counts.
Respondents must be independent within and across periods; outcome variances
may differ. These are asymptotic intervals, not finite-sample guarantees.

The honest interval additionally assumes that the population error of the
adjusted post-event forecast is bounded by the largest absolute corresponding
population reference error. Its empirical estimate is the displayed bias
bound. The procedure does not verify this assumption from data.

Every fitting window must identify all coefficients and retain positive
residual degrees of freedom. Constant covariates, collinear variables, or
factor levels missing from a fitting window cause a clear error. Consider
fewer substantively justified covariates or a longer defensible window; do
not silently discard problematic reference windows. Also inspect whether
forecast covariate distributions extend beyond those in the fitting windows.

Each pre-event and forecast period must have at least two complete responses.
The adjusted method does not borrow a variance for singleton periods. Small
samples and many predictors can still make uncertainty unreliable despite
satisfying the formal minimums. Missing outcome, time, or included covariates
cause omission with a warning; inspect the resulting period counts.

```{r effects}
plot(adjusted, type = "effects", inner_level = 0.90)
```

The report and extraction methods work as usual:

```{r}
coef(adjusted)
confint(adjusted)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
eventsurvey_report(adjusted, "adjusted-report.html")
```

`eventsurvey_summary()` remains time-only. Counts, outcome means, and outcome
variances, even with mean covariates, do not recover the joint respondent
information used by the adjusted estimator and its covariance calculation.
